reader_notes: Passage holds together as a coherent piece of British building-surveyor prose: torching is named, its purpose given, and the sting in the tail (damp passed to the battens) follows logically from 'mortar that touches timber passes damp to it'. Nothing read as factually wrong to me: lime-and-hair mortar applied to the tile backs from inside, tiles hung on nibs over battens with only every fourth course nailed, and felt superseding torching are all internally consistent and match the pre-1930s framing.

Cold-solved q1 as D on a single read. The last sentence before the felt line states it almost verbatim: 'whatever wet reached the torching sat against the battens until they decayed along its line.' No hesitation.

Distractors did their work without being unfair. A is the clean reversal (torching sheltered the battens and the timber stayed sound) and is actively contradicted. C over-reaches from the stated 'fine snow, dust and draughts' to 'whatever the weather drove against the roof' - tempting for a skimmer who latches onto 'At that job it worked'. B is the most interesting trap: torching is applied after hanging and the text mentions unnailed courses in the very next sentence, so a careless reader can stitch a causal link the passage never makes - the tiles are explicitly said to hang from the nibs.

Friction 1 - terminology density. Battens, courses, tiling, lugs, head, nibs, torching and felt all arrive inside eight sentences. The two least-guessable (torching, nibs) are glossed in place, so the question stays answerable, but this sits at the technical end for an ELF passage and a candidate will spend more of the clock on orientation than on the question.

Friction 2 - 'At that job it worked.' is a clipped four-word sentence whose 'at that job' means 'at that task'. Idiomatic in this register, but it made me re-read once to confirm it was not pointing at a job of work being carried out.

Friction 3 - tense shift in 'draughts that wind pushes up between the tiles' (present) inside an otherwise past-tense description. Reads as a generic-truth present, so defensible, but it is a small bump.

Minor ambiguity worth noting, not a blocker: 'Felt under the battens does the sheltering now' leaves the object of 'sheltering' implicit. The passage means the loft, but the phrasing is what makes option A's 'sheltered the battens' feel briefly available. Since D is stated outright, this never threatens the key.
The attributed byline 'Edith Gimberfold, building surveyor' carries an unusual surname, but the attribution format is unremarkable and did not affect the read.
